question: What is the oldest Christian doctrine? Where is the kingdom?
subtitle: The Two Ways, and the kingdom within
aliases: where is the kingdom of God
what did the first Christians believe
is the kingdom of heaven a place
how do I enter the kingdom
way of life and way of death
finding: The oldest recoverable teaching of the Jesus movement is not a creed. It is the Two Ways: there is a way of life and a way of death, and you choose by what you do. This is the framework Jesus taught (narrow gate, good tree, sheep and goats), the framework his community catechized converts in before baptism (Didache 1-6), and the framework the Jewish world around him already taught, Qumran included. In that framework the kingdom is not a postmortem destination you qualify for by believing the right thing. It is a present reality, within and among people, that most of them walk past without seeing. Salvation is participatory: you enter the way by walking it. We are pointing at the earliest documents the church itself produced and noting what is in them and what is not.
oneLiners: The oldest Christian document asks what you do. The modern church asks what you believe. Those are different religions wearing the same name.
He was asked how to inherit eternal life. He answered with commandments, in Matthew, in Mark, and in Luke. Nobody disputes the verses. They just don't preach them.
The kingdom isn't late. We're blind. That's his diagnosis, not mine. Thomas 113.
Before there was a creed, there was a choice.
Yes, the oldest Christian catechism has a late layer in it. The late layer is more ethics. Nobody ever went back and added a creed.
doNotSay: Don't count three salvation questions. It's two distinct scenes (the rich man, in all three Synoptics; the lawyer, Luke 10:25-28), triple-attested answers.
Don't quote Didache 1:3-2:1. That block is the sectio evangelica, widely held to be the latest layer. Quote 1:1-2, chapters 3-5, 4:14 and 6:2.
Don't say "chapters 1-6 are possibly pre-Pauline." The tradition in them is Jewish and pre-Christian; the compilation is composite, 50-120 CE.
Don't say Draper demonstrated direct textual continuity from Qumran into the Didache. Shared Jewish Two Ways tradition, not dependency.

sources.note: Asked the salvation question directly, he answers with commandments. Mark 10:17-19 and Luke 18:18-20 have it too.

sources.phrase: this do, and thou shalt live
sources.note: The lawyer's question, a separate scene: love God, love your neighbor, "this do, and thou shalt live." Independently at Mark 12:28-34 and Matthew 22:34-40.

The final judgment scene is entirely behavioral, and the sheep don't recognize who they served. No Markan parallel, and it gives Matthew, the evangelist of church order and confession, nothing. Redactors don't invent material that undercuts their own program.

sources.phrase: the kingdom of God is within you
sources.note: Present, local, now. "Among you" answers the traditional position just as well; Thomas 3 resolves the ambiguity by saying both.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 3 and 113
sources.note: "The kingdom is inside of you, and it is outside of you... it is you who are the sons of the living father." And 113: "spread out upon the earth, and men do not see it." Two independent streams agree on location and timing. The obstacle is perception, not chronology.

sources.title: Didache 1:1-2
sources.note: The oldest Christian catechism opens with the Two Ways, not a creed: love God, love neighbor, the negative Golden Rule. Chapters 1-6 are the entire entry requirement, and they are all behavior.

sources.title: Didache 4:14
sources.phrase: That is the way of life
sources.note: The catechism's own closing verdict on four chapters of conduct.

sources.title: Didache 6:2
sources.note: A floor and a direction of travel. The same point as Matthew 11:30, corroborated outside the gospels.

sources.title: 1QS 3:17-19 and 3:4-7, the Two Spirits
sources.note: Qumran, c. 100 BCE: two ways, mapped virtue and vice lists, expiation through inner transformation. Shared Jewish Two Ways tradition (with Barnabas 18-20 and the Doctrina Apostolorum), not textual dependency. The framework is demonstrably pre-Christian.

The Two Ways is continuous with the wisdom tradition. Agreed that it isn't distinctive; that is the point. If the distinctive doctrines were the heart of the message, they'd appear in the first thing converts were taught.

sources.title: Didache 1:3-2:1, the sectio evangelica
sources.note: "Your Didache quote is from the latest layer." Right about this passage, and we say so first (Niederwimmer, Kloppenborg). So don't lean on it. And notice: even the latest layer is still ethics. A second-century editor inserting Jesus-sayings produced more conduct material, not a creed.

sources.tier: red text · the future half of Luke 17
sources.note: "Verses 22-37 are explicitly future; you quoted 21 and stopped." Two addressees, two questions. Our position is both/and: present reality plus future consummation ("thy kingdom come," Matthew 6:10). What the Two Ways denies is a kingdom exclusively future, located elsewhere, entered by holding correct beliefs. Same exegesis as the rapture card.

"Works are the fruit of salvation, not its basis." That frame is read backwards from Romans. When Jesus draws the line he draws it at doing: "Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord... but he that doeth the will of my Father." Luke 6:46 likewise.

sources.title: Didache 14, the assembly's own sacrifice
sources.note: "The Didache is non-canonical, possibly late, and silence isn't an argument." Silence in the document whose purpose was to state what a convert must know before baptism is evidence. Chapter 14 does call the assembly's offering a thusia (Malachi 1:11): a sacrifice the community makes, not one Jesus paid. Concede it cleanly.
Jesus's brother, leading the Jerusalem church, states the conclusion flatly.

sources.phrase: Strive to enter in at the strait gate
sources.note: The narrow gate is in Luke as well as Matthew 7:13-14, so it is double tradition (Q 13:24), not single-source Matthew.
